title: What Democrats Could Learn from Blue Labour
author: Michael C. Behrent
content:
![What Democrats Could Learn from Blue
Labour](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-21-at-10.45.28
---PM.png)

As the left in most Western countries digs ever deeper into its decade-long
debacle, postmortems have become an increasingly prominent genre of left
discourse. One of the few genuinely lucid practitioners of this genre is
Maurice Glasman, the British peer and founder of [_Blue
Labour_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/long-live-blue-labour/), the
socially conservative and economically socialist current within the British
Labour party. In recent weeks, Glasman has frequently been asked to give his
opinion on the implosion of Keir Starmer's prime ministership. Amid all the
efforts to assess the reasons for Starmer's spectacular failure--foolish
mistakes, inept policy decisions, and plain old poor leadership--Glasman has
focused on the big picture: the fact that _labor parties_ have become
_progressive parties._

As Glasman explained in a [_recent
interview_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1QgxCTHYnbw&ref=compactmag.com)
with _The Spectator_ , "Labour was never a progressive party." Labour was
rooted in a working-class critique of the destructive effects of capitalism
and a moral outlook that was "more Methodist than Marxist." The most important
modern British progressive, in Glasman's view, was Margaret Thatcher, in the
sense that she sought to "insulate capitalism from political interference."
Tony Blair made the same creed palatable to Labour. As a result, says Glasman,
"Labour is dominated by progressives who as a matter of principle love global
capital." The unofficial anthem of progressivism is, in his opinion, John
Lennon's song "Imagine," with its fantasy of a world without countries,
religion, or a past.

In Glasman's view, this disdain for roots is entirely consistent (whatever
Lennon himself thought about "possessions") with the embrace of globalized
capitalism, which sees nations and traditions as so many obstacles to its
expansion. He believes that while Starmer had some redeeming qualities, his
core problem was that he was trained in international law, meaning that he
never had the formative political experiences in which Labour was once
grounded. For Starmer "reality was always a problem"--a statement that sums up
Glasman's broader critique of progressivism.
